preprocess_particles.name: preprocess_particles
preprocess_particles.description: Resize/crop a particle stack and optionally correct it for the CTF, to cut VRAM usage and speed up training

fields.name: md
fields.help: Xmipp/Relion metadata file with the images (+ alignments / CTF) to be analyzed

fields.name: sr
fields.help: Sampling rate of the input images, in Angstrom/pixel

fields.name: crop_box_size
fields.help: Real-space centred crop applied first. It trims the field of view without touching the sampling rate, which is useful to remove the empty padding around a particle before downsampling. A value larger than the input box zero-pads instead. NOTE: make sure the crop is wide enough to still contain the particle once its in-plane shift is applied.

fields.name: new_box_size
fields.help: Box size after Fourier resizing, applied after the crop. This is the parameter that trades resolution for speed and VRAM: halving the box divides the number of pixels (and roughly the memory a network needs) by four, while the new Nyquist frequency becomes 2 x sr x box_in / box_out Angstrom. The output sampling rate and the in-plane shifts stored in the metadata are updated accordingly.

fields.name: ctf_correction
fields.help:
none: leave the images untouched (default)
wiener: regularized CTF inversion, restoring amplitudes and phases
phase_flip: flip the sign of the frequencies where the CTF is negative, correcting phases only
NOTE: if you correct the CTF here, the images are already corrected, so downstream programs must be run with --ctf_type None to avoid correcting them twice.

fields.name: wiener_epsilon
fields.help: Fixed regularization constant for the Wiener filter. If not provided, an adaptive, per-image and frequency-dependent regularizer is estimated from the spectral SNR of each image, which is the recommended behaviour.

fields.name: batch_size
fields.help: How many images are processed at once (set by default to 1024). The CTF steps zero-pad each image by a factor of 2, so device memory scales with batch_size x (2 x box_out)^2; lower this value if you run out of memory, and monitor it with tools like nvidia-smi. Pass auto to let hax pick the largest batch that safely fits on your GPU (estimated analytically, without running anything, and capped at 2048). NOTE: use auto to make a large box fit, not to go faster. Unlike a training program, this one is bound by how fast images are read from disk, and its throughput is already flat above a batch of ~1024 - so on a box that fits comfortably, auto only adds a few seconds of extra compilation.

fields.name: device
fields.help: Where the images are processed. auto (default) uses the GPU when one is visible and falls back to the CPU otherwise. The GPU is several times faster than a many-core CPU here even counting the host/device transfers, so there is normally no reason to force cpu unless the GPU is busy with another job.

fields.name: num_read_workers
fields.help: Threads reading batches of images from disk ahead of the device. Raise it if the progress bar stalls on a slow or networked filesystem.

fields.name: num_write_workers
fields.help: Threads streaming the processed batches into the output stack.

fields.name: relative_image_paths
fields.help: Reference the output stack by its file name instead of its absolute path, so the output folder can be moved or shared. Metadata image paths are resolved against the working directory, not the metadata file, so with this flag downstream programs must be launched from inside output_path.

fields.name: output_path
fields.help: Path to save the preprocessed stack and its metadata

fields.name: config
fields.help: Path to a YAML/JSON file with parameter values (keys are the argument names without the leading '--'). Values from the file act as defaults; any argument also given on the command line overrides them. NOTE: the fully-resolved parameters (file + command line) are written to <output_path>/run_config.json on every run, and that file can be reused as a --config to reproduce the run.

preprocess_volumes.name: preprocess_volumes
preprocess_volumes.description: Resize/crop volumes (reference maps, masks) to match a preprocessed particle set

fields.name: vol
fields.help: One or more volumes to preprocess (reference maps, masks, initial volumes...). Pass several paths to process them all with the same settings, which is the way to keep a map and its mask consistent.

fields.name: sr
fields.help: Sampling rate of the input volumes, in Angstrom/pixel. If not provided, it is read from each volume's header.

fields.name: crop_box_size
fields.help: Real-space centred crop applied first. It trims the field of view without touching the sampling rate, which is how you remove the empty solvent padding around a map. A value larger than the input box zero-pads instead.

fields.name: new_box_size
fields.help: Cube size after Fourier resizing, applied after the crop. Use the same value you passed to preprocess_particles so that the volume and the images share a box size and a sampling rate.

fields.name: num_workers
fields.help: Threads used by the CPU FFT (-1, the default, uses every available core).

fields.name: output_path
fields.help: Path to save the preprocessed volumes

fields.name: config
fields.help: Path to a YAML/JSON file with parameter values (keys are the argument names without the leading '--'). Values from the file act as defaults; any argument also given on the command line overrides them. NOTE: the fully-resolved parameters (file + command line) are written to <output_path>/run_config.json on every run, and that file can be reused as a --config to reproduce the run.

hetsiren.name: hetsiren
hetsiren.description: Heterogeneous volume reconstruction with HetSIREN neural network

fields.name: md
fields.help: Xmipp/Relion metadata file with the images (+ alignments / CTF) to be analyzed. NOTE: If the metadata includes the label subtomo_labels, then TomoSIREN network will be trained (i.e., HetSIREN for tomography data). In this case, the parameter decoupling will not have any effect as pose/CTF decoupling is already handled by TomoSIREN.

fields.name: vol
fields.help: If provided, the neural network will learn how to refine this volume towards the heterogeneous states present in the images

fields.name: mask
fields.help: HetSIREN reconstruction mask (useful to focus the reconstruction/estimated landscape on a specific region of interest - the mask provided must be binary -  NOTE: since this is a reconstruction mask, it should be defined such that it covers the volume were the motions of interest are expected to happen)

fields.name: load_images_to_ram
fields.help: If provided, images will be loaded to RAM. This is recommended if you want the best performance and your dataset fits in your RAM memory. If this flag is not provided, images will be memory mapped. When this happens, the program will trade disk space for performance. Thus, during the execution additional disk space will be used and the performance will be slightly lower compared to loading the images to RAM. Disk usage will be back to normal once the execution has finished.

fields.name: sr
fields.help: Sampling rate of the images/volume

fields.name: lat_dim
fields.help: Dimensionality of the latent space of the network (set by default to 8)

fields.name: transport_mass
fields.help: When set, HetSIREN will be able to "move" the mass inside the mask instead of just reconstructing the volume. This implies that HetSIREN will estimate the motion to be applied to the points within the provided mask, instead of considering them fixed in space. This approach is useful when working with large box sizes that do not fit in GPU memory, or when a more through analysis of motions is desired. NOTE: When this option is set and a reference volume is provided, we recommend changing the reference mask to a tight mask computed from the reference volume. This mask now tells the program which regions should be moved. Therefore, consider providing a mask that covers all the protein regions you would like to be analyzed by HetSIREN.

fields.name: num_gaussians
fields.help: Before training the network, HetSIREN will try to fit a set of Gaussians in the reference volume to recreate it. The default criterium is to automatically determine the number of Gaussians neede to reproduce the reference volume with high-fidelity. However, if you prefer to fix the number of Gaussians in advance based on your own criterium (e.g., the number of residues in your protein), you can set this parameter. When set, the HetSIREN will fit this fixed number of Gaussians so that the reproduce the reference volume as well as possible.

fields.name: lattice_stride
fields.help:
Sub-sample the fixed-point lattice by this factor along each axis, keeping 1 / lattice_stride^3 of the sample points. The fixed-point decoder places one point per masked voxel, so the point count grows with the CUBE of the box: a 600 px box is ~13x the points of a 256 px one, and every per-particle tensor in the decode and render chain scales with it. This is the knob that makes a large box affordable (--lattice_stride 2 is an 8x reduction).
This trades resolution for memory: the sample spacing bounds the finest density CHANGE the decoder can express, to roughly 2 x lattice_stride x sampling_rate Angstrom. The consensus map is not affected -- it is carried by the reference amplitudes at full box sampling -- so this limits the heterogeneity, not the map you started from. The render width grows with HALF the spacing, which is what tiling costs; strides 1 and 2 therefore render exactly as before. Ignored when the points come from a Gaussian fit (see --num_gaussians), which sets the point count directly.

fields.name: render_chunk_size
fields.help:
Render the point cloud in blocks of this many points, summing the partial images and recomputing each block in the backward pass instead of keeping it live. The projection intermediates are the largest per-particle tensors in the training step -- they scale with batch_size x n_points -- and this caps them at batch_size x render_chunk_size instead. The rendered image is identical either way; the scatter is a sum over points, so this is exact and not an approximation. Costs roughly one extra render per step.
Use this to fit a large box on a smaller GPU (e.g. --render_chunk_size 262144). 0 (the default) renders the whole cloud at once, exactly as before. Smaller blocks save more memory and compile more slowly.

fields.name: local_reconstruction
fields.help: When set, HetSIREN will turn to local heterogeneous reconstruction/refinement mod, focusing the analysis of heterogeneity to a region of interest enclosed by the provided refernece mask. WARNING: IF PROVIDED, TRANSPORT MASS WILL BE OVERRIDDEN AND NOT CONSIDERED. WARNING: IF PROVIDED, HAVING A REFERENCE VOLUME IS MANDATORY. OTHERWISE, THIS PARAMETER WILL BE NEGLECTED.

fields.name: ctf_type
fields.help: Determines whether to consider the CTF and, in case it is considered, whether it will be applied to the projections (apply) or used to correct the metadata images (wiener - precorrect)

fields.name: mode
fields.help:
train: train a neural network from scratch or from a previous execution if reload is provided
predict: predict the latent vectors from the input images (reload parameter is mandatory in this case)

fields.name: epochs
fields.help: Number of epochs to train the network (i.e. how many times to loop over the whole dataset of images - set to default to 50 - as a rule of thumb, consider 50 to 100 epochs enough for 100k images / if your dataset is bigger or smaller, scale this value proportionally to it

fields.name: batch_size
fields.help: Determines how many images will be load in the GPU at any moment during training (set by default to 8 - you can control GPU memory usage easily by tuning this parameter to fit your hardware requirements - we recommend using tools like nvidia-smi to monitor and/or measure memory usage and adjust this value - keep also in mind that bigger batch sizes might be less precise when looking for very local motions - pass auto to let hax estimate the largest batch size that fits on your GPU (this maximizes GPU utilization, not necessarily accuracy)

fields.name: learning_rate
fields.help: The learning rate (lr) sets the speed of learning. Think of the model as trying to find the lowest point in a valley; the lr is the size of the step it takes on each attempt. A large lr (e.g., 0.01) is like taking huge leaps — it's fast but can be unstable, overshoot the lowest point, or cause NAN errors. A small lr (e.g., 1e-6) is like taking tiny shuffles — it's stable but very slow and might get stuck before reaching the bottom. A good default is often 0.0001. If training fails or errors explode, try making the lr 10 times smaller (e.g., 0.001 --> 0.0001).

fields.name: dataset_split_fraction
fields.help: Here you can provide the fractions to split your data automatically into a training and a validation subset following the format: training_fraction,validation_fraction. While the training subset will be used to train/update the network parameters, the validation subset will only be used to evaluate the accuracy of the network when faced with new data. Therefore, the validation subset will never be used to update the networks parameters. NOTE: the sum of training_fraction and validation_fraction must be equal to one.

fields.name: output_path
fields.help: Path to save the results (trained neural network, new metadata...)

fields.name: log_images_every
fields.help: How often (in epochs) to log the cheap intermediate results to Tensorboard: the predicted images and the central slices of the predicted volumes (set by default to 1, i.e. every epoch - set to 0 to disable)

fields.name: log_landscape_every
fields.help: How often (in epochs) to log the expensive intermediate results: the latent space embedding (Tensorboard projector), the intermediate volumes written to disk and the angular distribution plots (set by default to 5 - set to 0 to disable). NOTE: the embedding alone costs several seconds per call, so on small datasets it can easily dominate the training time - raise this value (or disable it) if logging is your bottleneck

fields.name: log_checkpoint_every
fields.help: How often (in epochs) to write the intermediate checkpoint used to resume an interrupted training (set by default to 5 - set to 0 to disable). This is deliberately independent from --log_landscape_every: how often you can resume should not be tied to how often you want pictures

fields.name: log_time_budget
fields.help: Self-tuning guard: the maximum fraction of the total wall clock that may be spent logging (e.g. 0.05 for 5%%). When the logging carried out so far exceeds this share of the run, the expensive tiers are skipped until training catches up. This adapts to dataset and box size on its own, which a fixed number of epochs cannot do (set by default to 0, i.e. disabled - the cadence flags alone decide)

fields.name: log_sync
fields.help: Log on the training thread instead of on a background one. By default the host-side logging work (Tensorboard writes, .mrc files, plots) is moved to a background thread so that it overlaps with the next epoch's GPU work rather than stalling it. Use this flag if you need the logs to be written in lockstep with training (e.g. while debugging)

fields.name: reload
fields.help: Path to a folder containing an already saved neural network (useful to fine tune a previous network - predict from new data - NOTE: If a reference volume was provided, HetSIREN also learns a gray level adjustment. In this case, reload must be the path to a folder containing two additional folders called: HetSIREN and Gaussian_volume_fitting)

fields.name: denoising_strength
fields.help: Determines how strongly HetSIREN will learn to remove noise from the resulting volumes. Increasing the value of this parameter will result in a stronger regularization of the noise, but it may affect the protein signal as well. (NOTE: We recommend setting this parameter in the range 0.0001 to 0.1)

fields.name: implicit_network
fields.help: When set, HetSIREN will use an implicit neural network approach to recover conformational states. Implicit neural networks are more memory consuming, but they are also more accurate in the detection of very local motions. If this architecture is selected, we strongly recommend to set as well the parameter total_mass to limit the memory consumption of the network and increase its performance.

fields.name: encoder_arch
fields.help:
Encoder that maps each image to its latent (set by default to convnn).
convnn / mlpnn both begin with a single dense layer over the FLATTENED image, Linear(box^2, ...), whose parameter count grows with the SQUARE of the box: at 320 px that one layer is ~105M parameters per encoder (~4.8 GiB once the two encoders, Adam and the EMA copy are counted), independent of batch size. This is what makes a large box run out of memory during training even when the batch is small.
convstem replaces that dense projection with a stack of strided convolutions that downsample the image to the same internal grid. Its parameter count is independent of the box (a few thousand), so training a 320 px box costs about what a 160 px box costs with convnn -- and it is translation-equivariant, which the dense projection is not. Recommended for large boxes on limited VRAM. NOTE: the three encoders are different architectures, so a checkpoint trained with one cannot be reloaded with another.

fields.name: pose_refine_reg
fields.help: Strength of the hinge that keeps the per-image rigid pose refinement within --pose_refine_max_angle of the input poses. It penalizes only the excess beyond that angle, so a genuinely-needed small correction is not pushed back to zero. Set to 0 to disable it.

fields.name: pose_refine_max_angle
fields.help: Deadzone (in degrees) of the pose-refinement hinge: rotations up to this angle are free, beyond it they are penalized with weight --pose_refine_reg. This is what 'stay a refinement' should mean -- do not wander further than a plausible alignment error. NOTE: setting it to 0 recovers the old one-sided pull towards the identity, which penalizes even the sub-degree corrections you want and biases the model into letting the decoder absorb the pose instead.

fields.name: shift_refine_reg
fields.help: Strength of the hinge on the per-image in-plane shift refinement, the exact analogue of --pose_refine_reg for translations. Set to 0 to disable. (NOTE: the shift refinement previously had no prior at all, even though a 2D image shift is exactly a 3D translation of the decoded object and is therefore the most trivially absorbable part of the refinement)

fields.name: shift_refine_max
fields.help: Deadzone (in pixels) of the shift-refinement hinge: shifts up to this magnitude are free, beyond it they are penalized with weight --shift_refine_reg.

fields.name: pose_refine_warmup_epochs
fields.help: Number of initial epochs over which the rigid pose refinement is ramped in from the identity. NOTE: the refinement heads are zero-initialized, so the model already starts at exactly the input poses -- the ramp buys nothing at initialization and only scales the pose head's gradient towards zero during precisely the window in which the decoder is learning to absorb the misalignment. It now defaults to 0 (refine from the first step); the decoder is instead held at a consensus early on, see --latent_warmup_epochs.

fields.name: latent_warmup_epochs
fields.help: Number of initial epochs over which the latent is ramped INTO the decoder (default: ~12%% of --epochs, so the schedule scales with the budget). For the first half of this window the decoder sees a zero latent, so it can only produce a single consensus volume -- and a consensus volume cannot absorb a per-particle pose error, so the whole misalignment has to be explained by the pose head. Over the second half the latent (and the KL term, which rides the same clock) ramps in linearly, against poses that have already been refined. This is the coarse-to-fine ordering a classical refinement uses -- consensus and poses first, heterogeneity after -- and it costs nothing. Set to 0 to feed the full latent from the first step.

fields.name: rigid_gauge
fields.help: Pins the decoder's per-particle output to a canonical frame, so a pose error cannot be absorbed by the decoder and has nowhere to go except the pose head (rotating the decoded object and refining the image pose produce the SAME projection, so without this the two are interchangeable -- and since every geometric prior here is rigid-invariant while the pose head is anchored to the identity, the decoder is the cheaper place for the model to put a misalignment). With --transport_mass the deformed cloud is rigidly superposed back onto the rest cloud (a weighted Kabsch, one 3x3 solve per particle); without it, the linearized rigid perturbations of the reference density are projected out instead. It does NOT remove motion: the correction is an isometry of the decoded object, so internal distances, hinge angles and relative domain motions are preserved exactly -- what it fixes is the FRAME the motion is reported in, and that frame is chosen by the weights: core (default) reweights against the residual so the frame is set by the least-moving part of the structure (the rigid core), which leaves domain motions entirely in the deformation field. mass uses the mass-weighted optimal superposition instead, in which a large domain motion makes the 'stationary' domain appear to counter-rotate and lets the pose head absorb a slice of the conformational change. off disables the correction but still reports the diagnostic, so a run can be checked for pose absorption without changing its behaviour. NOTE: without mass transport the gauge needs a reference density to differentiate, so it is unavailable (and silently a no-op) on fully ab-initio runs with no --vol.

fields.name: train_inverse
fields.help: When set, HetSIREN will additionally train an inverse decoder that maps the output Gaussian positions (the deformed point cloud produced by the decoder) back to latent vectors. This provides a direct point-cloud -> latent encoding that complements the image-based encoder. NOTE: this is only meaningful when mass transport is enabled (--transport_mass), since the Gaussian positions only move in that mode; if set without mass transport it is ignored.

fields.name: point_transformer
fields.help: When set, HetSIREN will use a point transformer architecture in the decoder (operating directly on the Gaussian point cloud) instead of the default decoder. NOTE: this option and --implicit_network are mutually exclusive; if both are provided, the implicit network takes precedence and this flag is ignored. Like the implicit network, it only takes effect with mass transport (--transport_mass).

fields.name: kl_lambda
fields.help: Weight (beta) of the VAE KL divergence, which regularizes the latent posterior towards a standard normal prior. Increase it for a smoother, more regularized latent space at the cost of reconstruction detail; decrease it (or set to 0) to let the encoder use the latent more freely. (NOTE: because the reduction changed, this is not comparable to any previously used constant). Setting it to 0 disables the variational machinery outright and trains a deterministic autoencoder. Pair any non-zero value with --kl_free_bits: on low-SNR data the KL's own optimum is an uninformative latent, and it will collapse to it.

fields.name: kl_free_bits
fields.help: Free-bits floor for the KL, in nats per latent dimension (default 0.5). A dimension whose KL has fallen below this stops being penalised, which removes the incentive to squeeze the last information out of the latent -- the failure mode (posterior collapse) where the encoder stops distinguishing particles and every one of them decodes to the consensus. It is a floor on the penalty, not on the information: a dimension the model has no use for is still free to stay unused, so a genuinely low-dimensional landscape is not forced to spread out. Raise it if the latent collapses, lower it (0 reproduces a plain KL) if the latent is noisy. Only used when --kl_lambda > 0.

fields.name: grad_clip_norm
fields.help: Global-norm gradient clipping threshold for the HetSIREN optimizer. Gradients whose global norm exceeds this value are rescaled down, which prevents occasional gradient spikes. Set to 0 to disable clipping.

fields.name: loss_type
fields.help: Reconstruction (representation) loss. mse (default): image-space L2 (robust on noise but blurs high frequencies). frc: Fourier Ring Correlation (sharp on clean data, but weights noise-dominated shells equally, so on experimental data it must be band-limited to a trusted resolution to avoid overfitting noise - see --freq_anneal_epochs and --sigma_anneal_factor, which together reproduce the EMAN2/e2gmm recipe of a band-limited FRC over a band-limited Gaussian representation). NOTE: the point transformer decoder always uses a Fourier-space loss (frc) regardless of this setting.

fields.name: freq_anneal_epochs
fields.help: Coarse-to-fine annealing: number of initial epochs over which the effective resolution is ramped in. During this window the decoder's first-SIREN-layer frequency (w0) and the upper limit of the FRC loss band are scaled up from --freq_anneal_start to full resolution (and, if --sigma_anneal_factor > 1, the Gaussian render width is annealed on the same clock). This forces the network to fit low-frequency structure before high-frequency detail, which strongly stabilizes training on noisy data (it prevents the SIREN from overfitting high-frequency noise early). Set to 0 to disable (train at full resolution from the first step). NOTE: does not affect the point transformer decoder's w0 (it has no SIREN first layer), but still anneals its loss band.

fields.name: freq_anneal_start
fields.help: Starting fraction (in (0, 1]) for --freq_anneal_epochs: freq_alpha begins at this value and ramps linearly to 1.0. Smaller values start coarser (lower resolution). Ignored when --freq_anneal_epochs is 0.

fields.name: sigma_anneal_factor
fields.help: EMAN2/e2gmm-style band-limited representation for the FRC loss. The Gaussian render width used in the training loss starts at sigma_anneal_factor x base_sigma (broad, low-resolution blobs) and shrinks back to the base width on the SAME coarse-to-fine clock as --freq_anneal_epochs. Broadening the Gaussians makes the density itself intrinsically band-limited early on, so the amplitude-invariant FRC cannot pour gradient into high-resolution noise shells the model is not yet allowed to represent (this is the safeguard that lets EMAN2 use FRC on experimental data). Only affects mass-transport rendering. Requires --freq_anneal_epochs > 0 (it shares that clock). Set to 1.0 to disable (default; fixed base width). Typical: 2-2.5 - the render blur uses a fixed 9-px kernel, so a broadened width beyond ~2.5x the base sigma is progressively truncated (still broadens, just sub-linearly), which bounds the useful range.

fields.name: schedule_recon_split
fields.help: Ramp the reconstruction split over training instead of holding it fixed. When set, the weight of the amplitude term ramps linearly from --recon_split_start to --recon_split_final over --recon_split_epochs (the motion term takes the complement). Starting near 0 makes early training explain the data almost purely by transport, so large motions organise before occupancy is allowed in. Only meaningful with mass transport (--transport_mass). Default: off (fixed --recon_split_final throughout).

fields.name: recon_split_start
fields.help: Amplitude-term weight at the START of training when --schedule_recon_split is on. 0.0 (default) means the data is explained purely by mass transport at the beginning.

fields.name: recon_split_final
fields.help: Amplitude-term weight at the END of the ramp (and the fixed weight used throughout when --schedule_recon_split is off). The reconstruction loss is w x L(learned amplitudes, frozen coords) + (1-w) x L(reference amplitudes, learned coords). The second term can only be reduced by moving mass, so it is what forces motion to be modelled as transport; the first lets occupancy explain the residual transport cannot, without being able to leak gradient into the coordinate head. Default 0.1 (90%% transport). Raise it toward 0.5 if genuine compositional change is being forced into motion; lower it toward 0 for pure transport.

fields.name: recon_split_epochs
fields.help: Number of initial epochs over which the amplitude-term weight ramps from --recon_split_start to --recon_split_final. Only used with --schedule_recon_split; if left at 0 the ramp falls back to the --freq_anneal_epochs clock.

fields.name: occupancy_l1
fields.help: Weight of the shrinkage half of the occupancy prior. Occupancy is what lets HetSIREN model compositional heterogeneity (a domain/ligand appearing or disappearing between particles) rather than forcing everything through the deformation field: each Gaussian carries a per-particle amplitude change on top of the reference. This term penalises how much of it there is, with a scale-normalised L1 (cost = fold change where the reference has density, so modulating existing density is cheap, while creating mass where the reference is empty costs |occ|/--occupancy_kappa -- possible but expensive). It is a mean over points, so it is on the same scale as --occupancy_tv. Only meaningful with mass transport (--transport_mass) and a reference. NOTE: this term only ever shrinks occupancy -- if the occ_fraction diagnostic collapses towards 0, this is too high.

fields.name: occupancy_tv
fields.help: Weight of the spatial-coherence half of the occupancy prior (graph total variation). It penalises occupancy differences between neighbouring Gaussians, so a whole domain switching on together pays only at its boundary while scattered per-Gaussian noise pays everywhere -- this is what separates a genuine compositional domain from amplitude noise, and it is the term to reach for if occupancy is coming out incoherent. Raise it for blockier occupancy, lower it toward 0 to allow finer-grained occupancy. Weighted independently of --occupancy_l1: coherent-but-large occupancy is a perfectly reasonable thing to ask for, so setting this alone (L1 at 0) is a normal configuration. Occupancy is active when either weight is > 0; with both at 0 (default) the amplitudes stay at the reference (pure mass transport).

fields.name: occupancy_kappa
fields.help: Creation threshold of the occupancy prior (as a density, in the reference's gray scale; default 0.05). It is added to the reference amplitude in the L1 denominator, so it sets how much evidence it takes to invent mass where the reference is (near) empty: smaller = harder to create mass, larger = easier. Where the reference already has substantial density it has little effect (the cost is a fold change). Only used when --occupancy_l1 > 0.

fields.name: occupancy_warmup_epochs
fields.help: Number of initial epochs over which occupancy is ramped in (default 3.0). While it ramps, the amplitudes stay at the reference so the data is explained purely by transport -- large motions organise first -- and occupancy is then released to explain only the residual that motion cannot (compositional change). Feeding occupancy from step 0 lets it short-circuit the motion (it is a strictly easier way to fit any image), so a non-zero warmup is recommended. Set to 0 to use occupancy from the first step. This ramp is independent of the occupancy priors -- it controls how occupancy enters the density, not how it is penalised -- so it applies whether or not --occupancy_l1/--occupancy_tv are set.

fields.name: arap_lambda
fields.help: Weight of the as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) deformation prior. Unlike the distance-preservation term, ARAP factors out the best local rotation per Gaussian before penalizing the deformation, so locally rigid motions (hinges, domain rotations) are NOT over-stiffened while noise-driven non-rigid shear is still resisted. Only active with mass transport and a reference volume. Set to 0 to disable (default); a small value (e.g. 0.05-0.2) is a good starting point, tuned together with --deformation_lambda/--distance_preservation_lambda.

fields.name: arap_rotation
fields.help: How the per-Gaussian optimal rotation in the ARAP prior (--arap_lambda) is recovered. polar (default) uses a matmul-only scaled polar iteration that is ~15-20x faster than the SVD path on GPU (batched 3x3 SVD is a severe XLA:GPU bottleneck) and numerically matches it to ~1e-6. svd uses the exact SVD; keep it as a reference/fallback (run both and compare the ARAP loss to self-check). No effect unless --arap_lambda > 0.

fields.name: geometric_lambda
fields.help: Weight of the geometric-correction loss. It penalises the local volume distortion of the heterogeneity decoder via the Gram determinant det(J_D(z)^T J_D(z)) of its Jacobian (the derivative of the decoded deformation w.r.t. the latent), pushing the decoded latent-to-shape map towards a locally volume-preserving (isometric) embedding. Set to 0 to disable (default). fields.name: decode_motion
fields.help: Include the deformation field (mass transport) when decoding. Combined with --decode_occupancy this gives the four ablations (both / motion only / occupancy only / consensus) needed to tell a genuine domain motion from an amplitude change: a real motion survives --no-decode_occupancy, real compositional change survives --no-decode_motion. fields.name: md
fields.help: Xmipp/Relion metadata file with the images (+ alignments / CTF) to be analyzed

fields.name: vol
fields.help: If provided, the neural network will start from this volume when assigning the angles and shifts to the images.

fields.name: mask
fields.help: ReconSIREN reconstruction mask (the mask provided must be binary - NOTE: since this is a reconstruction mask, it should be defined such that it covers the volume were the motions of interest are expected to happen)

fields.name: num_gaussians
fields.help: Before training the network, HetSIREN will try to fit a set of Gaussians in the reference volume to recreate it. The default criterium is to automatically determine the number of Gaussians neede to reproduce the reference volume with high-fidelity. However, if you prefer to fix the number of Gaussians in advance based on your own criterium (e.g., the number of residues in your protein), you can set this parameter. When set, the HetSIREN will fit this fixed number of Gaussians so that the reproduce the reference volume as well as possible.

fields.name: load_images_to_ram
fields.help: If provided, images will be loaded to RAM. This is recommended if you want the best performance and your dataset fits in your RAM memory. If this flag is not provided, images will be memory mapped. When this happens, the program will trade disk space for performance. Thus, during the execution additional disk space will be used and the performance will be slightly lower compared to loading the images to RAM. Disk usage will be back to normal once the execution has finished.

fields.name: sr
fields.help: Sampling rate of the images/volume

fields.name: do_not_learn_volume
fields.help: When this parameter is provided, ReconSIREN will just learn an angular assignment with shifts without learning any map. This is usually useful when a reference volume with high resolution is provided (e.g. coming from an atomic model) and no refinement of the map is needed.

fields.name: refine_current_assignment
fields.help: If your input metadata has already and angular assignment and shifts, you can provide this option to refine those angles instead of finding an ab initio alignment.

fields.name: do_not_use_anchor_rotations
fields.help: By default the poses proposed by the encoder are composed with a fixed set of anchor rotations spread on a spherical grid (one per pose hypothesis), which biases the ab initio pose search to cover orientation space more evenly. Provide this option to disable that composition.

fields.name: symmetry_group
fields.help: If your protein has any kind of symmetry, you may pass it here so that it is considered while learning the angular assignment and the volume (NOTE: only c* and d* symmetry groups are currently supported - the parameter is lower case sensitive - even if symmetry is provided, the network will learn a symmetry broken set of angles in c1. Therefore, the angles can be directly used in a reconstruction/refinement.)

fields.name: num_components
fields.help: Number of candidate pose hypotheses the pose encoder proposes per image during the ab initio search. For every image the network evaluates this many orientations (anchored on a spherical grid), renders a projection for each and keeps the best-matching one. A larger value covers orientation space more densely, making the pose search more robust to local minima, but increases GPU memory and compute roughly linearly (this is the main driver of ReconSIREN's training footprint). Set it lower to fit a smaller GPU at the cost of a coarser pose search. Default: 18.

fields.name: ctf_type
fields.help: Determines whether to consider the CTF and, in case it is considered, whether it will be applied to the projections (apply) or used to correct the metadata images (wiener - precorrect)

fields.name: mode
fields.help:
train: train a neural network from scratch or from a previous execution if reload is provided
predict: predict the latent vectors from the input images (reload parameter is mandatory in this case)

fields.name: epochs
fields.help: Number of epochs to train the network (i.e. how many times to loop over the whole dataset of images - set to default to 50 - as a rule of thumb, consider 50 to 100 epochs enough for 100k images / if your dataset is bigger or smaller, scale this value proportionally to it

fields.name: batch_size
fields.help: Determines how many images will be load in the GPU at any moment during training (set by default to 8 - you can control GPU memory usage easily by tuning this parameter to fit your hardware requirements - we recommend using tools like nvidia-smi to monitor and/or measure memory usage and adjust this value - keep also in mind that bigger batch sizes might be less precise when looking for very local motions - pass auto to let hax estimate the largest batch size that fits on your GPU (this maximizes GPU utilization, not necessarily accuracy)

fields.name: learning_rate
fields.help: The learning rate (lr) sets the speed of learning. Think of the model as trying to find the lowest point in a valley; the lr is the size of the step it takes on each attempt. A large lr (e.g., 0.01) is like taking huge leaps — it's fast but can be unstable, overshoot the lowest point, or cause NAN errors. A small lr (e.g., 1e-6) is like taking tiny shuffles — it's stable but very slow and might get stuck before reaching the bottom. A good default is often 0.0001. If training fails or errors explode, try making the lr 10 times smaller (e.g., 0.001 --> 0.0001).

fields.name: dataset_split_fraction
fields.help: Here you can provide the fractions to split your data automatically into a training and a validation subset following the format: training_fraction,validation_fraction. While the training subset will be used to train/update the network parameters, the validation subset will only be used to evaluate the accuracy of the network when faced with new data. Therefore, the validation subset will never be used to update the networks parameters. NOTE: the sum of training_fraction and validation_fraction must be equal to one.

fields.name: output_path
fields.help: Path to save the results (trained neural network, new metadata...)

fields.name: log_images_every
fields.help: How often (in epochs) to log the cheap intermediate results to Tensorboard: the predicted images and the central slices of the predicted volumes (set by default to 1, i.e. every epoch - set to 0 to disable)

fields.name: log_landscape_every
fields.help: How often (in epochs) to log the expensive intermediate results: the latent space embedding (Tensorboard projector), the intermediate volumes written to disk and the angular distribution plots (set by default to 5 - set to 0 to disable). NOTE: the embedding alone costs several seconds per call, so on small datasets it can easily dominate the training time - raise this value (or disable it) if logging is your bottleneck

fields.name: log_checkpoint_every
fields.help: How often (in epochs) to write the intermediate checkpoint used to resume an interrupted training (set by default to 5 - set to 0 to disable). This is deliberately independent from --log_landscape_every: how often you can resume should not be tied to how often you want pictures

fields.name: log_time_budget
fields.help: Self-tuning guard: the maximum fraction of the total wall clock that may be spent logging (e.g. 0.05 for 5%%). When the logging carried out so far exceeds this share of the run, the expensive tiers are skipped until training catches up. This adapts to dataset and box size on its own, which a fixed number of epochs cannot do (set by default to 0, i.e. disabled - the cadence flags alone decide)

fields.name: log_sync
fields.help: Log on the training thread instead of on a background one. By default the host-side logging work (Tensorboard writes, .mrc files, plots) is moved to a background thread so that it overlaps with the next epoch's GPU work rather than stalling it. Use this flag if you need the logs to be written in lockstep with training (e.g. while debugging)

reconstruct_volume.name: reconstruct_volume
reconstruct_volume.description: Consensus volume reconstruction from posed particles (single pass, with FSC denoising and gray scale calibration)

fields.name: md
fields.help: Xmipp/Relion metadata file with the images (+ alignments / CTF) to be analyzed

fields.name: sr
fields.help: Sampling rate of the images/volume

fields.name: ctf_type
fields.help: Whether the images carry a CTF. The reconstruction only needs to know if they do: apply, wiener and precorrect all mean they do (the slices are CTF weighted and the quotient deconvolves them), while None means they do not. NOTE: this must match your data -- weighting CTF-free images by a CTF is not a harmless no-op, it reweights the slices and degrades the map.

fields.name: tau
fields.help: Wiener floor of the reconstruction quotient (set by default to 0.05). This is only a numerical regularizer to keep the shells with little CTF power from blowing up -- the resolution of the map is set by the data, not by this. Raise it if the map looks noisy at high frequency, lower it if it looks over-smoothed.

fields.name: no_denoise
fields.help: Skip the FSC based denoising. By default the particles are split into two independent halves, the FSC between the resulting half maps measures the spectral signal-to-noise, and the combined map is filtered with it, so the shells carrying signal pass untouched and the shells that are only noise are removed (the measured resolution is printed). Pass this flag to get the raw, unfiltered map instead.

fields.name: no_gray_scale_calibration
fields.help: Skip the global gray-scale calibration. By default the finished map is forward-projected at a subset of the real poses and least-squares scaled against the input images, so that re-projecting it reproduces their contrast and value range. Pass this flag to keep the raw amplitudes.

fields.name: write_mask
fields.help: Also write a binary mask of the protein region derived from the reconstructed map (consensus_mask.mrc). This is the mask HetSIREN/MoDART expect in their --mask parameter.

fields.name: mask_threshold
fields.help: Only used with --write_mask: fraction of the map's maximum above which a voxel is considered protein (set by default to 0.02). Raise it for a tighter mask, lower it for a looser one.

fields.name: mask_dilate
fields.help: Only used with --write_mask: how many voxels to grow the mask by (set by default to 2), so that a deformation estimated later has somewhere to move the mass into.

fields.name: batch_size
fields.help:
How many images are read and inserted at once. The images are read on a thread pool while the GPU accumulates, so peak RAM tracks this value rather than the number of particles.
Left at auto (the default) the largest memory-safe batch is measured for your box and GPU before the pass starts - the measurement only compiles the kernel, so it allocates nothing and cannot itself run you out of memory. This matters because the cost per particle grows with the square of the box: a batch that is comfortable at 128 px needs ~7x the memory at 320 px. Pass an integer to pin it instead.

fields.name: threads
fields.help: Number of reader threads feeding the GPU with image chunks (set by default to 8). NOTE: on a spinning disk (HDD) several threads read different regions of the stack at once and the head seeks between them, so a lower value (1 or 2) can be faster there than the default.

fields.name: output_path
fields.help: Path to save the results (trained neural network, new metadata...)

fields.name: ssd_scratch_folder
fields.help: Path to a folder on a fast (SSD/NVMe) disk. The reconstruction has to read every particle once, so on a slow disk the read is the run: 1M particles at box 320 is 410 GB, which an HDD needs roughly an hour to deliver, and the GPU spends that hour idle. Given this parameter, the images are cached as a local float16 copy (half the bytes) and streamed from there. NOTE: building the cache still costs one full read of the original stack, so it does not make a single cold run faster - it pays off because the copy is reused, both by later runs and by the other hax programs (HetSIREN, Zernike3Deep, MoDART...) pointed at the same scratch folder, which build and read exactly the same cache.

fields.name: config
fields.help: Path to a YAML/JSON file with parameter values (keys are the argument names without the leading '--'). Values from the file act as defaults; any argument also given on the command line overrides them. NOTE: the fully-resolved parameters (file + command line) are written to <output_path>/run_config.json on every run, and that file can be reused as a --config to reproduce the run.

reconstruct_motion_corrected.name: reconstruct_motion_corrected
reconstruct_motion_corrected.description: Motion-corrected volume reconstruction by Fourier gridding, given a trained HetSIREN (single pass, with half maps and FSC) - the non-iterative alternative to modart

fields.name: md
fields.help: Xmipp/Relion metadata file with the images (+ alignments / CTF) to be analyzed

fields.name: sr
fields.help: Sampling rate of the images/volume

fields.name: ctf_type
fields.help: Whether the images carry a CTF. The reconstruction only needs to know if they do: apply, wiener and precorrect all mean they do, while None means they do not.

fields.name: motion_correction
fields.help: Path to a trained HetSIREN with mass transport (--transport_mass) checkpoint. Its encoder supplies each particle's latent and its decoder the displacement field that is removed from the image.

fields.name: tau
fields.help: Wiener floor of the reconstruction quotient (default 0.05). A numerical regularizer only -- the resolution is set by the data, not by this.

fields.name: correction
fields.help:
WHERE the modelled motion is removed (default image).
  image warps each 2D image and then inserts it normally. Fast -- one pass, a couple of operations per pixel -- but a projection ray gets ONE displacement, the density-weighted mean of the motion along it, because a single-valued 2D field cannot carry more. On the ribosome the part of the field that varies ALONG a ray measured ~95% of the part that does not, so this is a real approximation, not a rounding error.
  backprojection bends the backprojection rays in 3D instead: each canonical voxel reads the image where its own material landed, so two voxels at different depths on one ray read different pixels. This is what DynaMight does (Nat Methods 21, 1855-1862) and it is the geometrically correct version. It costs ~15-20x more (box x mask-fraction gathers per particle instead of one image warp).
  Both modes share the CTF weighting, the parity halves and the gray scale, so their maps are directly comparable and the difference between them IS the depth-resolved part of the motion.

fields.name: jacobian
fields.help: Multiply the resampled density by the Jacobian determinant of the deformation, making the correction conserve mass rather than values. Resampling alone moves intensities around; where a deformation compresses a region the same material lands on fewer pixels and must be scaled up for the line integral to survive. Second order for the near-isometric deformations the elastic priors produce -- measured at 1.2% (median) and 30% (p99) on the ribosome -- but it grows in proportion to the size of the motion. DynaMight does not do this. Off by default so the two correction modes reproduce their published behaviour unless asked.

fields.name: mask_radius
fields.help: Voxels within this many voxels of a consensus point that carries mass take part in the deformed backprojection (default 5.0); only used with --correction backprojection. Cost is linear in the number of selected voxels, and the model has nothing to say outside its own point cloud. The selected fraction is printed at startup.

fields.name: mask_taper
fields.help: Width, in voxels, over which the correction is faded out as it approaches the edge of that region (default 2.0, raised cosine). Do not set this to 0 unless you want to see why it exists: the correction is a difference, so ending it at a hard boundary leaves a step of its full size, and that step rings through the Fourier division. Measured with no taper, 71.6% of the entire difference between the corrected map and the consensus sat in a +-1.5 voxel shell at the mask edge -- 5.1% of the box by volume, where it was 1.43x the size of the density itself. The interpolated field does not fade on its own (its outermost band is the largest of any), so the window has to impose it. Full-strength correction therefore reaches to --mask_radius minus this.

fields.name: warp_sigma
fields.help: Width, in pixels, of the smoothing applied when the scattered per-point displacements are turned into a dense image-plane warp (default 2.0). It should be comparable to the spacing between the model's points in projection; too small leaves gaps between them, too large washes out the boundary between a moving domain and a static one.

fields.name: min_coverage
fields.help: Pixels whose splat coverage falls below this fraction of the mean are left UNWARPED rather than having a warp extrapolated into them (default 0.05). Doing nothing where the model has no support is the safe default; dividing by a near-zero coverage is how the previous 3D field transfer produced displacements thousands of Angstrom long.

fields.name: no_denoise
fields.help: Skip the FSC-based denoising of the combined map. The FSC is still measured and reported.

fields.name: no_gray_scale_calibration
fields.help: Skip the global gray-scale calibration against the input images.

fields.name: also_consensus
fields.help: Also reconstruct the ordinary (uncorrected) consensus from the same particles and print both resolutions. Strongly recommended: it is the control that says whether the motion correction changed anything, and it is the only way to attribute a difference to the correction rather than to any other part of the pipeline.

fields.name: write_mask
fields.help: Also write a binary mask of the protein region derived from the reconstructed map.

fields.name: batch_size
fields.help: How many images are read per chunk (default 512). Peak RAM tracks this rather than the particle count.

fields.name: field_batch
fields.help: How many particles are pushed through the motion decoder at once (default 32). This is the VRAM-sensitive number -- the decoder holds (particles x points x hidden) activations -- so lower it if the field decode runs out of memory. It does not change the result.

fields.name: threads
fields.help: Number of reader threads feeding the GPU (default 8). On a spinning disk a lower value can be faster.

fields.name: output_path
fields.help: Path to save the results (trained neural network, new metadata...)

fields.name: ssd_scratch_folder
fields.help: When the parameter load_images_to_ram is not provided, we strongly recommend to provide here a path to a folder in a SSD disk to read faster the data. If not given, the data will be loaded from the default disk.

fields.name: config

Values from the file act as defaults; any argument also given on the command line overrides them. NOTE: the fully-resolved parameters (file + command line) are written to <output_path>/run_config.json on every run, and that file can be reused as a --config to reproduce the run.
